components.note: 亻 (person) — 保 relates to a person looking after or protecting someone, originally a caretaker holding a child.
呆 (dāi) gives a hint of the sound — 保 is pronounced bǎo, a connection that has shifted over time.

example.hanzi: 公司决定保留这个部门。
example.pinyin: Gōngsī juédìng bǎoliú zhège bùmén.
example.english: The company decided to keep this department.
example.fact: 保留 covers both a concrete sense ("keep, retain an object") and an abstract one ("hold back an opinion," as in 保留意见, "reservations") — a duality that traces back to 保's core sense "to protect, keep safe" plus 留's "to remain, stay behind," so retaining a stance and retaining an object share the same verb.

components.note: 夂 (a foot, to walk) — 各 pictures people arriving from different directions.
口 (mouth) — different people speaking gave 各 its meaning 'each' or 'every,' emphasizing individual distinctness.
禾 (grain/rice plant) — 种 relates to seeds and planting crops.
中 (zhōng) gives the sound — 种 is pronounced zhǒng, matching aside from tone.

example.pinyin: Chāoshì lǐ yǒu gèzhǒng shuǐguǒ.
example.english: The supermarket has all kinds of fruit.
example.fact: 各种 always sits directly before a noun (各种水果, "all kinds of fruit"), unlike English "various," which can also stand alone after a linking verb ("the reasons are various") — Chinese needs a different construction, like 各不相同 or 各种各样, to make that same claim without a following noun.

components.note: 土 (earth/soil) — 在 originally related to standing on the ground
才 (cái) gives the sound — 在 is pronounced zài, a close match
宀 (roof) — 家 is about a home, the space under a roof.
豕 (shǐ, 'pig') supplies the ancient sound for 家; keeping a pig under one's roof was also a practical sign of a household in ancient China, though the modern readings jiā and shǐ no longer rhyme.

example.pinyin: Zhōumò wǒ yìbān zàijiā kàn shū.
example.english: On weekends I usually stay home reading.
example.fact: 在家 drops the possessive or measure marker an ordinary noun would need (contrast the fuller 在我的家里) — here 家 behaves almost like a location adverb rather than a regular noun, the same pattern seen in 在校 ("at school") and 在职 ("employed, on the job").

components.note: 目 (eye) — 眼 refers directly to the eye itself.
艮 (gèn) gives a sound hint — 眼 is pronounced yǎn; the rhyme has drifted apart over the centuries.

example.hanzi: 眼前的困难只是暂时的。
example.pinyin: Yǎnqián de kùnnan zhǐshì zànshí de.
example.english: The difficulties in front of us now are only temporary.
example.fact: 眼前 literally means "in front of the eyes" (眼 "eye" + 前 "front") — from that concrete image it extended to mean "right now, at present," the same visual-to-temporal leap English makes when it calls something "right before us."

components.note: 目 (eye) — 冒 originally described something extending over or covering, related to a covering over the head.
冃 (mào) is an exact match for the sound of 冒.
犭 (dog) — 犯 originally related to a dog attacking, later extended to any act of violation
㔾 (jié) gives a sound distantly related to 犯's reading fàn, having drifted apart over time

example.pinyin: Wǒ búshì gùyì yào màofàn nǐ.
example.english: I didn't mean to offend you.
example.fact: 冒犯 is noticeably more formal than everyday words for anger like 生气 — it's the word reached for in a careful apology or a description of a breach of etiquette, closer to the register of English "to give offense" than to a blunt "to piss someone off."

components.note: 示 (altar) — 禁 relates to sacred restrictions observed near an altar.
林 (lín) reflects the character's historical phonetic root, though the modern reading jìn has diverged.
止 depicts a footprint, with toes at the top and the leg below — a simple picture of a foot, later extended to mean 'to stop.'

example.pinyin: Zhèlǐ jìnzhǐ xīyān.
example.english: Smoking is prohibited here.
example.fact: 禁止 is the standard wording on official signs and regulations (禁止吸烟, "no smoking"; 禁止停车, "no parking") — that formal, rule-based register sets it apart from personal, spoken alternatives like 不许 or 不让 ("[a person] won't allow it"), even though all three can be translated "not allowed."

components.note: 扌 (hand) — relates directly to 持's meaning 'to hold, maintain.'
寺 (sì) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from chí.
纟 (thread) — 续 relates to continuing, like an unbroken thread
卖 (mài) gives a loose sound connection to 续's reading xù

example.pinyin: Dàyǔ chíxù le sān tiān.
example.english: The heavy rain continued for three days.
example.fact: 持续 describes something continuing without a break over a stretch of time, and pairs naturally with a duration (持续三天, "lasted three days") — its near-synonym 继续 instead emphasizes resuming or carrying on an activity after a pause, a distinction that's easy to blur since English "continue" covers both.

components.note: A short stroke placed above a longer one — a simple graphic way to show 'up' or 'above,' contrasted with 下 (down), which flips the strokes.

example.pinyin: Táishàng de yǎnyuán chàng de hěn hǎo.
example.english: The performer on stage sang very well.
example.fact: 台上 follows the common noun+上 pattern for "on/at" a location (桌上, "on the table"; 车上, "in the car"), but 台 narrows specifically to a raised platform — so 台上 always implies a stage or dais, not just any flat surface.

components.note: 氵 (water) — the sea or river being traveled through
斿 — a banner streaming in the wind, evoking free, drifting movement
氵 (water) — 泳 describes moving through water.
永 (yǒng) gives the sound — an exact match with 泳.

example.pinyin: Tā měitiān zǎoshang qù yóuyǒng.
example.english: He goes swimming every morning.
example.fact: 游泳 is often analyzed as a verb-object compound (游 "to swim, roam" + 泳 "a swim") rather than one indivisible verb — that's why a duration phrase can be inserted between the two syllables in fuller sentences (游了两个小时的泳, "swam for two hours"), the same separable pattern found in 睡觉 and 唱歌.

components.note: 电 (simplified from 電) depicts a bolt of lightning — since lightning is a natural form of electricity, the character came to mean 'electricity.'
A simple drawing of a swaddled baby — arms reaching out, legs bundled together in a wrap.

example.pinyin: Wǒ gèng xǐhuan kàn diànzǐ shū.
example.english: I prefer reading e-books.
example.fact: 电子 literally means "electric particle" (电 "electricity" + 子, here a noun suffix for small discrete units, as in 原子 "atom") — the same 子 that means "child" in words like 孩子 also does this unrelated grammatical job of marking a tiny particle.

meanings: unable to do anything about it

components.note: 氵 (water) — 没 originally meant to sink or drown in water, later extended to the negative 'not have.'
殳 (shū) is the historical sound component; it no longer rhymes with méi in modern Mandarin, another case of sound drift over time.
氵 (water/stream) — water naturally follows a fixed course, an image linked to the idea of 'law' or 'method.'
去 (to go/a course) — the path a stream follows suggested a regulated, consistent way of doing things, hence 'law, method.'

example.pinyin: Tā méifǎ jiějué zhège wèntí.
example.english: He has no way to solve this problem.
example.fact: 没法 is a colloquial contraction of 没有办法 ("there's no method/way") — everyday speech regularly compresses a longer set phrase down to its most essential syllables, the same kind of shortening behind 别 (from 不要) and 甭 (from 不用).

components.note: 犭 (animal) — 猴 names an animal, the monkey.
侯 (hóu) gives the sound — an exact match with 猴.
A simple drawing of a swaddled baby — arms reaching out, legs bundled together in a wrap.

example.pinyin: Hóuzi xǐhuan chī xiāngjiāo.
example.english: Monkeys like eating bananas.
example.fact: The 子 in 猴子 is doing pure grammatical work, marking 猴 as a countable animal noun, the same role it plays in 兔子 ("rabbit") and 鸭子 ("duck") — none of these are literally anyone's "child," unlike 孩子, where 子 still carries its original sense.

components.note: Woman/girl — shows this relates to a female figure.
Jade — suggests something precious and beautiful, like a treasured baby.
Woman/girl — shows this relates to a female figure.
Jade — suggests something precious and beautiful, like a treasured baby.

example.hanzi: 这个娃娃是我妹妹最喜欢的玩具。
example.pinyin: Zhège wáwa shì wǒ mèimei zuì xǐhuan de wánjù.
example.english: This doll is my little sister's favorite toy.
example.fact: 娃娃 reduplicates 娃, which on its own already means "baby, young child" — doubling a syllable like this is a common Mandarin strategy for coining an affectionate, singsong word for something small and endearing, the same instinct behind baby-talk pet names like 猫猫 or 狗狗.

components.note: 氵 (water) — 没 originally meant to sink or drown in water, later extended to the negative 'not have.'
殳 (shū) is the historical sound component; it no longer rhymes with méi in modern Mandarin, another case of sound drift over time.

example.pinyin: “Duìbuqǐ!” “Méishì, méi guānxi.”
example.english: "Sorry!" "It's fine, no worries."
example.fact: 没事 swings between two almost opposite everyday uses: reassuring someone that a mishap is "no big deal," and describing having free time (我没事, "I'm not busy") — both senses fall out naturally from the same literal meaning, "there is no matter/business going on."

components.note: 纟 (silk/thread) — 经 originally referred to the vertical warp threads in weaving.
工 (gōng) gives a related sound cue for 经 (jīng), reflecting an older, closer pronunciation link between the two.
氵 (water) — 济 originally meant 'to cross a river,' extended to 'to help, aid; economy.'
齐 (qí) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from jì.

example.hanzi: 这个国家的经济发展很快。
example.pinyin: Zhège guójiā de jīngjì fāzhǎn hěn kuài.
example.english: This country's economy is developing quickly.
example.fact: 经济 is generally believed to have entered modern Chinese via a Japanese coinage (経済, keizai) that repurposed two Classical Chinese characters — 经 ("to manage, regulate") and 济 ("to aid, benefit") — to translate the Western concept of "economy," one of many modern terms that traveled from Chinese characters to Japan and back again.

components.note: 辶 (walking/movement) — relates to 达's meaning 'to reach, arrive, achieve.'
大 (dà) gives the sound — 达 is pronounced dá, a close match sharing the same rhyme.

example.pinyin: Shuāngfāng zhōngyú dáchéng le xiéyì.
example.english: The two sides finally reached an agreement.
example.fact: 达成 almost always takes an abstract object — an agreement, a goal, a consensus (达成协议, 达成目标) — rarely a physical destination, a job usually left to 到达 or 抵达 instead, even though all three share the root 达 ("to arrive at").

components.note: 艹 (grass, plant) — 芝 names a type of grass and plant.
之 (zhī) gives the sound — an exact match with 芝.
力 (strength) — 加 pictures adding one's effort to a cause.
口 (mouth, words) — combining strength with words of support gave 加 its meaning 'to add' or 'to increase.'
哥 doubles the character 可 ('to approve, to sing'), originally suggesting a call-and-response song between two singers; the meaning later narrowed to 'elder brother.'

example.hanzi: 他下个月要搬到芝加哥工作。
example.pinyin: Tā xià gè yuè yào bāndào Zhījiāgē gōngzuò.
example.english: He's moving to Chicago for work next month.
example.fact: 芝加哥 is a pure phonetic transliteration: each character (芝 "iris/fungus," 加 "to add," 哥 "elder brother") was chosen only to approximate the English sound, with no attempt at meaning — the standard method Chinese uses for foreign place names with no natural semantic equivalent.

components.note: 大 (a grown man) — the figure being depicted.
一 (a hairpin) — worn across the top of the head to mark a coming-of-age ceremony, giving 夫 its meaning 'man, husband.'
女 (woman) forms the left side of the character.
彐 depicts a broom — a woman holding a broom, a traditional image of housework, gave 妇 its meaning 'married woman, wife.'

example.hanzi: 这对夫妇结婚三十年了。
example.pinyin: Zhè duì fūfù jiéhūn sānshí nián le.
example.english: This couple has been married for thirty years.
example.fact: 夫妇 reads a shade more formal and written than the everyday 夫妻, and it almost always pairs with the measure word 对 (一对夫妇, "a couple") rather than 个 — a small detail that underscores a couple being counted as one bonded unit rather than two separate people.

components.note: 广 (a wide, open building) — a hall or pavilion
坐 (to sit) — a seat placed inside the building
亻 (person) — 位 relates to a person's location.
立 (to stand) — the spot where a person stands gave 位 its meaning 'position' or 'place,' and later, a polite measure word for people.

example.pinyin: Qǐng bǎ zuòwèi rànggěi lǎorén.
example.english: Please give up your seat for the elderly.
example.fact: 座位 literally joins "seat" (座, a raised place to sit) with "position" (位) — the same 位 that serves as a polite measure word for people (三位客人, "three guests") shows up here instead marking a location, a reminder of how flexibly one character can drift between counting people and naming the spot they occupy.

components.note: 冖 (a covering/roof) — represents the building or schoolhouse where learning happens.
子 (child) — 学 depicts children gathered to study.
⺍ is a small graphic element at the top of the character; its original pictorial meaning, if any, has been lost over time.
阝 (a mound/enclosure) — relates to 院's meaning 'courtyard, institution,' an enclosed place.
完 (wán) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from yuàn.

example.pinyin: Tā zài yīnyuè xuéyuàn xué gāngqín.
example.english: She studies piano at the music conservatory.
example.fact: 学院 sits a notch below 大学 ("university") in China's usual naming conventions — it typically names a specialized college or faculty (音乐学院, "music conservatory"; 医学院, "medical school") rather than a full university, so translating it simply as "university" can overstate the institution.

components.note: The character traces the front view of an ox's head, with the top stroke and crossing lines representing its curved horns and ears.
女 (woman) — 奶 relates to a woman nursing, and to milk.
乃 (nǎi) is an exact match for the sound of 奶.

example.hanzi: 我早饭喜欢喝一杯牛奶。
example.pinyin: Wǒ zǎofàn xǐhuan hē yì bēi niúnǎi.
example.english: I like to drink a glass of milk for breakfast.
example.fact: 牛奶 spells out the animal up front — 牛 ("cow") + 奶 ("milk") — where English "milk" defaults to cow's milk unless stated otherwise; that's why other kinds need their own explicit compound in Chinese, like 羊奶 ("goat's milk") or 豆奶 ("soy milk"), rather than a qualifier added to a generic base word.

components.note: 辶 (to walk) — 逃 means to escape or flee, involving movement.
兆 (zhào) gives a rhyme close to táo, with the initial shifted.
土 (here representing a person swinging their arms, not its usual meaning 'earth') — depicts someone in motion.
止 (a foot) — combined with the moving figure above, 走 shows a person walking or running.

example.pinyin: Xiǎotōu chènluàn táozǒu le.
example.english: The thief fled in the confusion.
example.fact: 逃走 pairs 逃 ("to flee") with 走, which here works not as its own full verb but as a directional complement meaning "away" — the same role 走 plays in 拿走 ("take away") and 跑走 ("run away"), a common resultative pattern in Mandarin verb compounds.

components.note: ⺼ (flesh/body) — historically linked to physical strength and overcoming an opponent
生 (shēng) gives a sound close to 胜's reading shèng, sharing a similar historical pronunciation

example.pinyin: Zhōngguó duì zài juésài zhōng huòshèng.
example.english: The Chinese team won in the final.
example.fact: 获胜 is distinctly more formal and written than the everyday 赢 ("to win") — it shows up in sports commentary and news headlines, while 赢 dominates casual speech (我赢了, "I won"), a register split worth tracking when choosing between the two.

components.note: A single horizontal stroke — the simplest possible way to represent the number one; some traditional interpretations link it to heaven or earth as the very first stroke of creation.
面 was originally a pictograph of a human face, with an outline around an eye — later broadening to mean 'face, surface, side.'

example.pinyin: Tā yímiàn zǒulù, yímiàn chàng gē.
example.english: She walked and sang at the same time.
example.fact: 一面's most common job in modern speech isn't "one side" at all, but half of the paired construction "一面...,一面..." ("while... at the same time..."), used to describe two actions happening together — a grammatical use built on the more literal meaning "one face/aspect" of something running alongside another.

components.note: 爫 (a hand, claw-like) — reaching to pick something.
木 (tree) — a hand picking fruit from a tree gave 采 its meaning 'to pick, gather, collect.'
又 (a hand) — reaching to take hold of something.
耳 (ear) — from an ancient battlefield practice of taking a fallen enemy's ear as proof of a kill, the origin of 取's meaning 'to take, obtain.'

example.pinyin: Zhèngfǔ cǎiqǔ le xīn de cuòshī.
example.english: The government adopted new measures.
example.fact: 采取 only ever takes abstract objects like measures, actions, or attitudes (采取措施, "adopt measures"; 采取态度, "take a stance") — it can't mean physically "picking something up," a job left to its component 采 alone (as in 采花, "to pick flowers") or to a plain verb like 拿.

components.note: 毛 (hair) — 毫 originally meant a fine, thin hair.
疋 — a person walking, shown pausing and looking back uncertainly
矢 (an arrow/cane) — an old man's walking stick, held while hesitating
口 (mouth) — 问 relates to speaking, specifically asking a question.
门 (mén) gives a hint of the sound — 问 is pronounced wèn, related but the tone and vowel have shifted.

example.hanzi: 毫无疑问,他是这次比赛最优秀的选手。
example.pinyin: Háowúyíwèn, tā shì zhè cì bǐsài zuì yōuxiù de xuǎnshǒu.
example.english: Without a doubt, he is the best competitor in this competition.
example.fact: 毫无疑问 is built from 毫 ("the tiniest amount," originally "a fine hair") negated by 无 ("without") plus 疑问 ("doubt, question") — literally "not the slightest hair of doubt," the same intensifying use of 毫 that appears in 毫不 ("not in the least") to negate something as completely as possible.

components.note: 亲 (here representing a tree, related to 榛/hazel) — 新 pictures a tree being cut.
斤 (an axe) — freshly chopping wood gave 新 its meaning of something 'new' or 'fresh.'
女 (woman) — 娘 names a female relative, mother or young woman.
良 (liáng) gives a sound close to niáng, sharing the same rhyme.

example.hanzi: 新娘穿着一件白色的婚纱。
example.pinyin: Xīnniáng chuānzhe yí jiàn báisè de hūnshā.
example.english: The bride is wearing a white wedding dress.
example.fact: 新娘 literally means "new mother/woman" (新 "new" + 娘, an old word for "mother" or young woman) — its counterpart 新郎 ("bridegroom") pairs the same 新 with 郎, an old term for a young man, so the two wedding words are built on matching "new + gendered elder-term" patterns from opposite sides.

components.note: 土 (earth) — 型 originally related to a mold made of clay used for casting
刑 (xíng) gives the sound — 型 is also pronounced xíng, an exact match

example.hanzi: 这部电影属于喜剧类型。
example.pinyin: Zhè bù diànyǐng shǔyú xǐjù lèixíng.
example.english: This movie belongs to the comedy genre.
example.fact: 类型 is the more technical, classificatory word for "type" — common in genres, models, and data categories (电影类型, "film genre"; 数据类型, "data type" in programming) — where the plainer, everyday 种 (as in 各种, also in this batch) covers "kind" in casual conversation.

components.note: 贝 (shell, an ancient form of money) — 购 relates to spending money to buy something.
勾 (gōu) gives a sound close to gòu, sharing the same syllable body and differing mainly in tone.
牛 (ox/cattle) — cattle were among the earliest and most valuable kinds of property, connecting 物 to the general idea of 'object' or 'thing.'
勿 (wù) gives the sound — 物 is also pronounced wù, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Zhōumò wǒ dǎsuàn qù gòuwù.
example.english: I plan to go shopping this weekend.
example.fact: 购物 is a formal, written-register verb-object compound (购 "to purchase" + 物 "goods") that shows up in signage and compounds like 购物中心 ("shopping mall") — everyday spoken Chinese more often reaches for the plainer 买东西 ("to buy things") to say the same thing.

components.note: 旦 (dàn) gives the sound — 但 is also pronounced dàn, an exact match.
心 (heart) — 愿 relates to a heartfelt wish or desire
原 (yuán) gives a loose sound connection to 愿's reading yuàn

example.pinyin: Dànyuàn míngtiān shì gè hǎo tiānqì.
example.english: I only wish tomorrow's weather will be good.
example.fact: 但愿 opens a sentence to express a hope for something the speaker can't control or isn't confident about — unlike 希望 ("to hope"), which freely takes a subject and object (我希望你...), 但愿 behaves more like a fixed interjection, closer to English "if only" than to an ordinary verb.

components.note: 金 depicts a bell or metal casting mold, with dots representing droplets of molten metal — a picture linked to metal and, later, specifically gold.
尸 (body) — ties to 属's sense of belonging to a category or class of related things
禹 (yǔ) gives a loose sound connection to 属's reading shǔ

example.pinyin: Zhè bǎ yǐzi shì jīnshǔ zuò de.
example.english: This chair is made of metal.
example.fact: 金's modern default sense has narrowed toward specifically "gold" (金子) in most everyday compounds — 金属 preserves the character's older, broader meaning by adding 属 ("category, class"), literally "the metal category," so the general sense of "metal" survives alongside the newer, narrower one.

components.note: 纟 (silk/thread) — 绿 originally described a shade of green-dyed silk.
录 (lù) gives a sound close to lǜ, sharing the same syllable body and differing mainly in tone.
⺈ (a person, bent over) — the figure whose outward expression is being depicted.
巴 — traditionally linked to desire or emotion, so together the character points to a person's expression or complexion, extended to 色's meaning 'color, appearance.'

example.pinyin: Tā xǐhuan chuān lǜsè de yīfu.
example.english: She likes wearing green clothes.
example.fact: 绿 is one of the relatively few Mandarin syllables that requires the umlaut ü, written lǜ — since lu and lü are distinct syllables in Pinyin (English "u" has no such counterpart), learners typing without an ü key, or simply mishearing the vowel, often garble it as "lu4" instead.

meanings: variant of 抽菸|抽烟[chou1 yan1]

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 抽 describes pulling something out with the hand.
由 (yóu) gives a sound distantly related to chōu, having drifted apart over time.
火 (fire) — smoke, 烟's meaning, rises from fire.
因 (yīn) gives a rhyme close to yān, with the tone shifted.

example.pinyin: Yīshēng jiànyì tā búyào chōuyān.
example.english: The doctor advised him not to smoke.
example.fact: 抽烟 literally means "to draw/pull smoke" (抽 "to pull out" + 烟 "smoke") — the same verb 抽 used for drawing a card from a deck (抽签) or drawing water up from a well, here applied to pulling smoke into the lungs.

meanings: to take part in an election

components.note: 立 (to stand) pictures a person standing firm.
兄 (elder brother, here a rival) suggests standing up against someone, giving 竞 its meaning 'to compete, to contend.'
辶 (to walk/move) — 选 relates to the process of selecting, as if moving through options
先 (xiān) gives a sound close to 选's reading xuǎn

example.pinyin: Tā juédìng jìngxuǎn shìzhǎng.
example.english: He decided to run for mayor.
example.fact: 竞选 combines 竞 ("to compete, contend") with 选 ("to select, elect") — literally "to compete to be selected" — and it almost always takes the office being sought directly as its object (竞选总统, "to run for president"), with no preposition needed the way English inserts "for."

components.note: 王 (a variant form of 玉, meaning jade) — 理 originally referred to the natural grain or pattern in jade, later extending to 'reason, logic, to manage.'
里 (lǐ) gives the sound — 理 is also pronounced lǐ, an exact match.

example.pinyin: Zhège jiàgé hěn hélǐ.
example.english: This price is very reasonable.
example.fact: 合理 literally means "fitting with reason" (合 "to fit, match" + 理 "reason, logic"); its opposite 不合理 ("unreasonable") is formed by simply adding 不 in front — one of several everyday adjectives built directly on 理 ("logic, principle"), alongside 道理 ("sense, reason") and 理论 ("theory").

components.note: 木 (wood) — 检 originally related to a wooden tally or label used for checking records
佥 (qiān) gives a sound distantly related to 检's reading jiǎn, having drifted apart over time
氵 (water) — 测 originally referred to measuring the depth of water.
则 (zé) gives a rhyme close to cè, with the tone and initial shifted.

example.hanzi: 医院对样本进行了检测。
example.pinyin: Yīyuàn duì yàngběn jìnxíng le jiǎncè.
example.english: The hospital tested the sample.
example.fact: 检测 leans technical and instrument-based — lab tests, medical screenings, sensor readings (病毒检测, "virus testing") — where its near-synonym 检查 covers the broader everyday sense of "to check, inspect," like checking luggage or homework, a split that roughly maps onto English "to detect" versus "to check."

components.note: 宀 (roof/house) — relates to 完's meaning 'complete, finish,' as in a fully built house.
元 (yuán) was the phonetic base; the pronunciation later shifted to wán, so only a partial rhyme remains today.
虫 (a small creature) — 蛋 names an egg, historically grouped together with small creatures like insects and reptiles.
延 (yán) is only distantly related in sound to dàn — the connection has drifted apart to the point of being barely recognizable.

example.hanzi: 如果考试再不及格,我就完蛋了。
example.pinyin: Rúguǒ kǎoshì zài bù jígé, wǒ jiù wándàn le.
example.english: If I fail the exam again, I'm done for.
example.fact: 完蛋 is a colloquial idiom, not a literal statement about eggs — 完 ("finished") plus 蛋 ("egg") together evoke something "cracked, done for, ruined," in the same register as English slang "cooked" or "toast"; it's casual and best avoided in formal writing.

components.note: 月 (moon) — 期 relates to time measured by the moon's cycles, like a period or term.
其 (qí) gives a hint of the sound — 期 is pronounced qī, a connection that has shifted slightly in tone.
门 (door/gate) — 间 pictures light passing through an entryway.
日 (sun) — sunlight shining through a gap in a doorway gave 间 its meaning of a space 'in between,' as in 中间 (in the middle) or 时间 (time, the space between moments).

example.hanzi: 春节期间,很多商店都不营业。
example.pinyin: Chūnjié qījiān, hěn duō shāngdiàn dōu bù yíngyè.
example.english: During the Spring Festival period, many stores are closed.
example.fact: 期间 almost always attaches after another noun to mean "during [that period]" (春节期间, "during Spring Festival"; 假期期间, "during the holiday") rather than standing alone as a general word for "time" — for that broader sense, Chinese reaches for 时间 instead.

components.note: 舟 (boat) — 航 relates to traveling by boat, and later by extension, air or space travel
亢 (kàng) gives a sound distantly related to 航's reading háng, having drifted apart over time
王 here is a variant of 玉 (jade), appearing once on each side of the character.
刂 (knife) — cutting a piece of jade in two, symbolizing a division into groups, gave 班 its meaning 'class, group.'

example.hanzi: 我们的航班延误了两个小时。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen de hángbān yánwù le liǎng gè xiǎoshí.
example.english: Our flight was delayed two hours.
example.fact: 航班 specifically names a scheduled flight identified by a number (航班号, "flight number") — for the general idea of air travel or the aircraft itself, Chinese uses 飞机 or 航空, reserving 航班 strictly for the scheduled-service sense, closer to English "flight 205" than to "airplane."

components.note: Originally depicted a burning candle or the sun's rays radiating outward — the source of 白's meaning 'white, bright, clear.'
⺈ (a person, bent over) — the figure whose outward expression is being depicted.
巴 — traditionally linked to desire or emotion, so together the character points to a person's expression or complexion, extended to 色's meaning 'color, appearance.'

example.hanzi: 他今天穿了一件白色的衬衫。
example.pinyin: Tā jīntiān chuān le yí jiàn báisè de chènshān.
example.english: He wore a white shirt today.
example.fact: Beyond the color itself, 白色 carries a historical political charge: 白色恐怖 ("White Terror") describes state violence against leftist movements, following the same international convention — also used for the "White" forces in the Russian Civil War — of pairing white with anti-revolutionary factions, as the opposite of red's association with communism.

components.note: 心 was originally a pictograph of the physical shape of a human heart, and came to represent the mind, feelings, and intention as well.
A vertical line 丨 running through the middle of a box or flag 口 — a simple image for the idea of 'center, middle.'

example.pinyin: Tā xīnzhōng chōngmǎn le gǎnjī.
example.english: Her heart was filled with gratitude.
example.fact: 心中 literally means "inside the heart" (心 "heart" + 中 "middle, inside") and reads as a more literary, introspective way to say "in one's heart/mind" — its plainer everyday counterpart is 心里, built the same way but with 里 ("inside") in place of 中.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — 嘴 refers directly to the mouth, or a beak-like spout.
觜 (zī) gives a sound distantly related to zuǐ, having drifted apart over time.
田 (farmland) over 土 (earth/soil) — originally referred to a village or a measured unit of farmland, later extended to mean 'inside' or a unit of distance.

example.pinyin: Tā zuǐlǐ hánzhe yí kuài táng.
example.english: He had a piece of candy in his mouth.
example.fact: 嘴里 extends past its literal "inside the mouth" to describe reported speech, as in 从他嘴里听说的 ("heard it from him") — treating the mouth as the source of words, a metonymy that also shows up in the more formal, literary 口中, built on 口 (the classical word for mouth) instead of the everyday 嘴.

components.note: 八 (to divide/split) — represents something being separated into smaller parts.
亅 (a hook/line) — cutting a small piece off, an image tied to the meaning 'small, tiny.'
钅 (metal) — 镇 originally referred to a heavy metal weight used to press something down, later extending to 'garrison town.'
真 (zhēn) gives the sound — an exact match with 镇's reading zhèn, differing only in tone.

example.pinyin: Zhège xiǎozhèn fēngjǐng hěn měi.
example.english: This small town has beautiful scenery.
example.fact: 镇 names a specific level in China's administrative hierarchy — below a county (县) but above a village (村) — so 小镇 isn't just a vague descriptor but points to a real category of town-level unit, a more precise use than how loosely English "small town" tends to get applied.

components.note: 厂 (chǎng) gives a hint of the sound — 产 is pronounced chǎn, nearly identical apart from the final consonant.
口 (mouth), stacked three times — many mouths talking about or judging something, the source of 品's meaning 'product, item; quality, rank.'

example.hanzi: 这家公司的产品质量很好。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiā gōngsī de chǎnpǐn zhìliàng hěn hǎo.
example.english: This company's products are of great quality.
example.fact: 产品 joins 产 ("to produce") with 品 ("item" — itself three stacked 口 "mouth" components, suggesting many voices judging or discussing something) to give the neutral business term for anything manufactured, distinct from 商品, which specifically emphasizes an item as merchandise bought and sold.

components.note: 米 (grain, especially husked rice) — 精's meaning 'refined, essence, spirit' relates to rice refined to its purest form.
青 (qīng) gives a sound hint — 精 is pronounced jīng, sharing the same rhyme though the initial consonant differs.
力 depicts the blade of a plow — since plowing fields took great physical effort, the shape came to represent strength or power.

example.pinyin: Niánqīngrén jīnglì chōngpèi.
example.english: Young people are full of energy.
example.fact: 精力 refers specifically to a person's physical or mental stamina — the energy to get through a task or a day — while the physics sense of "energy" (kinetic, electrical) uses the unrelated word 能量 instead, a distinction easy to miss since English "energy" covers both.

components.note: 辶 (to walk) — 退 relates to moving backward or away
艮 (gèn) gives a sound distantly related to 退's reading tuì, having drifted apart over time
亻 (person) leans to the side.
木 (tree) — a person resting against a tree gave 休 its meaning 'to rest.'

example.pinyin: Wǒ yéye qùnián tuìxiū le.
example.english: My grandfather retired last year.
example.fact: 退休 literally means "to withdraw and rest" (退 "to withdraw, retreat" + 休 "to rest") — 休 is itself a picture of a person 亻 leaning against a tree 木, giving the word an almost literal image of stepping back to finally relax after a working life.

components.note: 木 (tree) — traditionally read as a tree that has borne fruit.
立 (standing) — standing close by to watch it grow, evoking closeness and nurture, extended to 亲's meaning 'close, dear; parent, relative.'
宓 depicts stillness and quiet beneath a roof.
山 (mountain) — a quiet, secluded mountain gave 密 its meaning 'dense, secret, close.'

example.pinyin: Tāmen liǎ guānxì hěn qīnmì.
example.english: The two of them have a very close relationship.
example.fact: 亲密 describes emotional closeness between people (亲密关系, "intimate relationship") — worth not confusing with the visually similar 亲近 (a milder word for growing familiarity) or 亲自 ("in person, personally"), which despite looking related has nothing to do with closeness at all.

components.note: 礻 (spirit, altar) — 礼 relates to ceremony and rites performed before the spirits.
乚 reflects the character's phonetic root, though its exact link to the modern reading lǐ is unclear today.
豸 (a beast) suggests physical form.
皃 (an old form meaning 'face, appearance') combines with the beast radical, giving 貌 its meaning 'appearance, looks.'

example.pinyin: Gēn zhǎngbèi shuōhuà yào yǒu lǐmào.
example.english: You should be polite when speaking with elders.
example.fact: 礼貌 combines 礼 ("ritual, etiquette," built on the altar/spirit radical 礻, tied to formal ceremony) with 貌 ("appearance, looks") — literally something like "the outward form of proper conduct," which is why 有礼貌 ("polite," lit. "having politeness") treats good manners as a visible quality one possesses.

components.note: 土 (earth/soil) — 地's original meaning is 'earth, ground'
也 (yě) gives a partial sound match for 地's other reading dì; in this grammatical-particle usage the character is instead pronounced 'de'
A short stroke placed below a longer one — the mirror image of 上 (up), together forming a simple, opposite pair.

example.hanzi: 这座城市有一个地下停车场。
example.pinyin: Zhè zuò chéngshì yǒu yí gè dìxià tíngchēguǎn.
example.english: This city has an underground parking garage.
example.fact: 地下 extends from its literal "below ground" sense to anything secret or operating outside official channels — 地下工作 ("underground work," covert political activity) and 地下经济 ("underground economy") borrow the same spatial metaphor English uses for "underground" resistance or black markets.

components.note: ⺼ (flesh) — 胡 originally referred to the flesh under an animal's chin or throat
古 (gǔ) gives the sound — an exact match with 胡's reading hú
讠 (speech radical) — shows 说 relates to talking or language
兑 (duì) is the phonetic component; historically 说 was also pronounced closer to 兑's sound before shifting to shuō

example.pinyin: Bié húshuō, zhè búshì zhēn de.
example.english: Don't talk nonsense, that's not true.
example.fact: 胡 in 胡说 traces back to an old, disparaging term for non-Han peoples of Central Asia (as in 胡人) — that historical sense of "foreign, other, hence wild or unruly" survives in several unrelated-looking compounds like 胡乱 ("carelessly, haphazardly") and 胡闹 ("to act foolishly, make a scene").
